summary_paragraph: Mr. ___, a man with primary progressive multiple sclerosis, neurogenic bladder with a suprapubic catheter, and a history of recurrent multidrug-resistant urinary tract infections, was admitted due to persistent fevers and malaise despite outpatient treatment with Bactrim for a suspected UTI. He presented with dizziness and weakness but no urinary symptoms. Initial evaluation showed no leukocytosis, and imaging revealed no abscess or obstructive uropathy. Urine culture grew Proteus mirabilis, resistant to Bactrim but susceptible to piperacillin-tazobactam. He was treated with IV antibiotics, transitioned to IV ceftriaxone, and discharged on oral cefpodoxime for a 10-day course. During admission, he was evaluated for dysphagia, with speech and swallow recommending a ground diet and supervised feeding. His stage II-III sacral and ischial pressure ulcers were managed with debridement and wound care, and plans were made for home support including a new mattress and cushion. Anemia and skin flaking were managed supportively. He was discharged home with services, stable and improving.
